title: I'm 45 and my home is paid off. Should I start investing in property, in Penang or the Klang Valley?
excerpt: A 45-year-old Penang mother with a paid-off home asks whether to start investing, and where. Sean says it depends on her ambition and appetite for risk, and that units with several ways to let are safest.

question.asker: From Q, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Q, 45, lives in Penang, is married with two children, has no loans and her home is fully paid; she is in the top 20% income group and already has fixed deposits, shares, unit trusts and ETFs. Agents have pitched her units under RM600,000 in Kuala Lumpur, including a 300 sq ft studio near KLCC aimed at short stays. The Klang Valley seems to offer better yields and more choice, but she doesn't know the area and worries about managing a property from afar.
question.text: Should she buy investment property at her age rather than other investments, and is the Klang Valley or Penang the better choice?

answer.quote: The more options I have for a particular property, the more confidence I have.
answer.summary: Only if she wants to grow more for her family and can stomach the risk; if she is already comfortable, she doesn't need to. At 45 her loans will be shorter, so rent rarely covers the instalment and she should expect to put more cash down. The Klang Valley offers more, but only if she is willing to travel and manage it, and she should favour units that can be let in several ways.

reasons.title: Shorter loans change the maths
reasons.body: Banks lend until about 65 to 70, so she would get around 20 years rather than 35, and residential rents rarely cover such instalments. Many older investors simply borrow 30% to 50% and pay the rest in cash.

reasons.title: Her paid-off home is a safety net
reasons.body: It can be refinanced in an emergency, which lets her take a little more risk. The questions are her ambition, how much loss she could bear, and whether she enjoys property enough to research it.

reasons.title: Rents follow jobs
reasons.body: Penang homes are expensive and mostly owner-occupied, so rents are low, except in Batu Kawan, where new factories have drawn workers. The Klang Valley still draws graduates from across Malaysia, keeping rents higher.

reasons.title: Several ways to let protect you
reasons.body: A unit that suits families, working couples, short stays and room-by-room letting has fallbacks if one market fails. A 300 sq ft studio at about RM2,000 per sq ft relies on short stays, and its long-term rent and resale are harder.

actions: Decide whether you need more wealth or are content, and how much of a price fall you could live with.
If you buy, plan to put down enough cash that the shorter loan stays comfortable.
View about 20 properties, including subsales in person, before choosing.
Prefer units that can be let long-term, furnished for medium stays, short-term or by the room.
Furnish the unit well; few owners in a building do, and it widens your choice of tenants.
caveat: If travelling to manage a Klang Valley unit would be a burden, Sean suggests other investments, or studying Batu Kawan closer to home. He mentions a project he booked through FAR Capital, a property investment club he is a VIP member of.
sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #209. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in April 2023. The episode was sponsored by Dreame, an unrelated vacuum cleaner brand; Sean also points viewers to FAR Capital, a property investment club he is a VIP member of.
